::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Find your way around the course project; load a real Movebank GPS
track; plot it; count fixes per day; compute daily distances; find the gaps.

**Time:** ~60 minutes. **Packages:** `readr`, `dplyr`, `lubridate`, `ggplot2`.
:::

## Task 0 — Orientation

Open `animtrack-2627.Rproj` in RStudio. Everything in the course assumes you
work *inside* this project, so that paths like `data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz`
resolve without editing anything.

```
animtrack-2627/
├── data/        ← the tracks and rasters we use all course
├── classes/     ← one folder per session: slides.qmd + exercise.qmd
├── R/           ← small helper scripts (simulators, Session 5 onwards)
└── docs/        ← the rendered website — do not edit by hand
```

Check that your installation works:

```{r}
#| eval: false
need <- c("sf", "terra", "amt", "adehabitatLT", "adehabitatHR", "ctmm",
          "momentuHMM", "bcpa", "circular", "tidyverse")
for (p in need) {
  ok <- requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("%-13s %s\n", p, if (ok) as.character(packageVersion(p)) else "** MISSING **"))
}
```

Anything `MISSING`? Go back to the [setup page](../../setup.qmd) now.

## Task 1 — Load the track

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

raw <- read_csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)

dim(raw)
names(raw)[1:6]
```

Two things to notice. `read_csv()` keeps Movebank's hyphenated column names,
so you need backticks to refer to them. And it has already parsed `timestamp`
as a date-time:

```{r}
class(raw$timestamp)
tz(raw$timestamp)
```

Tidy it into the four columns every movement analysis needs:

```{r}
track <- raw |>
  transmute(
    id  = `individual-local-identifier`,
    t   = timestamp,
    lon = `location-long`,
    lat = `location-lat`
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |>
  arrange(id, t)

track
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Always know your time zone

`read_csv()` assumed **UTC**, which is right for Movebank. A CSV from another
source may be in local time; parse it explicitly with
`ymd_hms(x, tz = "Africa/Johannesburg")`, and convert to UTC with
`with_tz()`. Mixing the two is the commonest silent error in movement analysis.
:::

### Your turn

**1a.** How many animals, and how many fixes each?
**1b.** Over what period?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
track |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(fixes = n(), from = min(t), to = max(t),
            days = round(as.numeric(difftime(max(t), min(t), units = "days"))),
            .groups = "drop")
```

Six buffalo, followed for very different lengths of time. Any summary that
pools them is dominated by whoever contributed most fixes.
:::

## Task 2 — Plot it

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(track, aes(lon, lat, colour = id)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.25, alpha = 0.7) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Longitude (°)", y = "Latitude (°)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Six buffalo, Kruger National Park") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-important}
## This plot is subtly wrong

`coord_equal()` makes one degree of longitude as long as one degree of
latitude. At 24.5°S a degree of longitude is only
`r round(111.32 * cos(24.5 * pi / 180))` km, against ~111 km for latitude, so
the map is stretched east–west by about 10%. At Kruger's latitude that is
tolerable; for a track spanning 7°N to 54°N it is not. Session 2 fixes this
properly with coordinate reference systems.
:::

## Task 3 — Fixes per day

A collar is programmed to attempt a fix on a schedule. Counting fixes per day
tells you how well it kept to it.

```{r}
per_day <- track |>
  mutate(day = as_date(t)) |>
  count(id, day, name = "fixes")

per_day |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(median_per_day = median(fixes), max_per_day = max(fixes),
            .groups = "drop")
```

### Your turn

**3a.** Plot fixes per day over time for each animal.
**3b.** Some days have *more* fixes than the schedule allows. Why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(per_day, aes(day, fixes)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1f6f78", width = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ id, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Fixes per day") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The programmed schedule is roughly 24 per day. Days far above it are
**duplicates**: the collar re-transmitted fixes it had already sent.

```{r}
track |>
  count(id, t) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  summarise(duplicated_timestamps = n(), extra_rows = sum(n - 1))
```

Thousands of repeated timestamps. We remove them properly in Session 3; for now
note that **you only find this by looking**.
:::

## Task 4 — Daily distance

Straight-line distance between consecutive fixes, summed per day. Because our
coordinates are in degrees we need a **great-circle** distance. Here is the
haversine formula written out — Session 2 replaces it with `sf`, which does
this properly on the ellipsoid.

```{r}
haversine_m <- function(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2, r = 6371008.8) {
  to_rad <- pi / 180
  dlat <- (lat2 - lat1) * to_rad
  dlon <- (lon2 - lon1) * to_rad
  a <- sin(dlat / 2)^2 + cos(lat1 * to_rad) * cos(lat2 * to_rad) * sin(dlon / 2)^2
  2 * r * asin(sqrt(a))
}

steps <- track |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE) |>          # drop duplicates first
  group_by(id) |>
  mutate(dist_m = haversine_m(lag(lon), lag(lat), lon, lat),
         dt_h   = as.numeric(difftime(t, lag(t), units = "hours"))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(!is.na(dist_m))

daily <- steps |>
  mutate(day = as_date(t)) |>
  group_by(id, day) |>
  summarise(km = sum(dist_m) / 1000, steps = n(), .groups = "drop")

daily |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(median_km_per_day = round(median(km), 1), .groups = "drop")
```

### Your turn

**4a.** Plot daily distance over time for one animal.
**4b.** Is a day with 6 fixes comparable to a day with 24?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

Queen's collar was patchy, which makes her the instructive case:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-align: center
daily |>
  filter(id == "Queen") |>
  ggplot(aes(day, km)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = steps >= 22), size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#1f6f78", `FALSE` = "firebrick"),
                      labels = c(`TRUE` = "complete day (22+ steps)",
                                 `FALSE` = "incomplete day")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Distance per day (km)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Queen: daily distance") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

No, they are not comparable. Summed distance is a **lower bound** that depends
on how many fixes you had — the modifiable temporal unit problem from the
slides:

```{r}
daily |>
  filter(id == "Queen") |>
  mutate(steps_that_day = cut(steps, c(0, 6, 12, 21, Inf),
                              labels = c("1–6", "7–12", "13–21", "22+"))) |>
  group_by(steps_that_day) |>
  summarise(days = n(), median_km = round(median(km), 1))
```

Days with only a handful of fixes come out at a third of the distance of
complete days — for a reason that has nothing to do with the buffalo. Before
comparing days, keep only complete ones or, better, resample to a regular
interval (Session 3).
:::

## Task 5 — Find the gaps

```{r}
gaps <- steps |>
  filter(dt_h > 3) |>
  arrange(desc(dt_h)) |>
  transmute(id, from = t - dhours(dt_h), to = t, gap_days = round(dt_h / 24, 1))

gaps |> slice_head(n = 8)

gaps |> count(id, name = "gaps_over_3h")
```

### Your turn

**5a.** Visualise the gaps as a timeline for all animals.
**5b.** Name three biological or technical reasons for a long gap.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(steps, aes(t, id)) +
  geom_point(shape = "|", size = 3, alpha = 0.15, colour = "#1f6f78") +
  geom_segment(data = gaps |> filter(gap_days >= 1),
               aes(x = from, xend = to, y = id, yend = id),
               colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Fixes (teal) and gaps longer than a day (red)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Common causes of long gaps:

- **Battery** — schedules that deliberately pause, or a collar running flat
- **Habitat** — dense canopy, gorges and burrows block the satellites
- **Collar orientation** — an animal lying on the antenna
- **Data transfer** — the data exist on the collar but were never downloaded
- **Mortality or drop-off** — the collar keeps reporting the same place, or stops

The first three are the ones that bias analyses: they are not random, they
depend on where the animal is and what it is doing.
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
You compute `diff(t)` on a data frame you forgot to sort by time. What do you
get?

- [ ] An error
- [x] A mixture of positive and negative intervals, and nonsense summaries
- [ ] Correct intervals — `diff()` sorts internally
- [ ] All zeros

::: {.quiz-feedback}
`diff()` subtracts each element from the next, in the order given. Out of
order, you get negative time differences, and any speed computed from them is
garbage — often silently, because `summary()` still returns numbers. **Always
`arrange(id, t)` before any step calculation.**
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A collar programmed for hourly fixes returns 14,000 fixes over exactly two
years. Roughly what was the fix success rate?

- [ ] ~100%
- [x] ~80%
- [ ] ~50%
- [ ] Impossible to say without the DOP values

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Two years of hourly attempts is 2 × 365 × 24 ≈ 17,520. 14,000 / 17,520 ≈
**80%**, a fairly typical figure for a large mammal in mixed habitat. And the
20% that failed is not noise if failures concentrate in closed habitat.
:::
:::
